column2: The masons have begun raising your observatory on the highest ground you hold. Lenses must come from the glassworks of Nuln or Tilea, brass dials from the guild smiths, and star tables from any scholar willing to part with them. It will take some time before all is ready.
I can't wait!

Your observatory is finally ready. The dome opens on a clear night, Mannslieb rides pale and steady above the hills, and the stars lie scattered across the dark like spilled salt. With great anticipation you take your seat at the great lens.
I wonder what I will discover.

You have spent many nights at the lens. The Sun's road, the slow wheel of Mannslieb, the wandering stars the Celestial wizards name and read... and then there are the other things. Lights that are there and then are not. Morrslieb, green and sickly, rising where no table says it should. So many questions, and only one lifetime to ask them.

You have spent many nights at the lens, and the sky has never once been the same twice. The Changer of Ways writes in the stars as in all things, and every road is His. Will you chart the turning of the spheres and learn the laws that bind them, or seek the lights that move against all law?

You have spent many nights at the lens. The Slann taught that the Old Ones set the stars in their places as a scribe sets glyphs on a plaque, and that the Great Plan can be read in their turning. Yet some lights do not keep the Plan, and the green moon that came with the Rift grows fat on something else entirely.

Few Dawi trouble themselves with the sky, and the younger beards laughed when you raised a dome on the peak above the hold. But the ancestors read the stars to time their seasons long before the Umgi learned to count, and now, with frost in your beard and a brass lens at your eye, you begin to see why.
How do the heavens move?
Is there something... strange out there?

Night after night you mark the lights on your tables, and patterns emerge. The wandering stars loop back on themselves as if the sky were bent around another centre than the one the priests teach. You begin to wonder whether the Known World truly lies at the heart of it all.
Interesting...

Your nights at the observatory are proving deeply fascinating, but the work has outgrown your lenses. A finer glass, a new dial and a library of older star tables would let you push much further, though none of it comes cheap.
I must move forward!
No, this is proving too expensive.

One morning your [GetFromRelation] [From.GetTitledFirstName] comes to see you, pale from a sleepless night. 'I am worried for you,' [From.GetSheHe] says. 'They say you spend every night in that tower, and that you have begun to say the world is not where [From.Religion.GetRandomGodName] placed it. Men have burned for less. Please, stop this, for your own sake.'
Don't worry, I'm fine...
Stay out of my business!
It is not what you think. I am only... writing poetry.

Your nightly studies of the heavens teach you a great many things. Angles and distances, the way a lens bends light, the reckoning of hours by the stars: your engineers and gunners are already putting your tables to use. You feel closer to understanding the order of the world.
I sense a harmony out there...

Lately the observatory brings only frustration. A lens cracked in the frost, weeks of cloud, servants and pigeons wandering in at the worst moment, and a sky that refuses to agree with your tables. It is very hard to keep your mind on the work.
I must persist. The truth is out there.
It's no use!

[Root.GetTitledName],

It has come to my attention that you pursue studies which deny the order that [Root.Religion.GetRandomGodName] has set upon the world. I am certain such rumours are slander, and that one of your standing would never stoop to the kind of stargazing that leads men to witchcraft and the pyre. Were they true, however, I would be most disappointed, and the faithful would not long remain silent.

In the name of [Root.Religion.GetRandomGodName],
[From.GetTitledName]
The [From.GetTitle] should mind [From.GetHerHis] own temple!
The best answer to this is silence.
I must not challenge the faith.

Your studies of the celestial spheres progress beyond anything you dared hope. You see movements and relationships no table has ever recorded, and it seems clear to you that the laws which move the stars must also move the world beneath them.
And what is the world?

You are certain now. It cannot be otherwise. The world is round, it turns about the Sun, and pale Mannslieb turns about the world as a hound circles its master. Only Morrslieb keeps no law at all, and you do not like to think about what that means. How little the priests know of the heavens!

You are certain now. The world is round, it turns about the Sun, and pale Mannslieb turns about the world as a hound circles its master. Your priests nod as you explain it, as if you had told them the sky is blue: the gods wrote this in the heavens for any who would look. Only Morrslieb keeps no law at all, and on that even they fall silent.
I must publish my findings!
I will continue my studies in secret.
I will stop with this achievement.
No! This is the whisper of the Dark Gods!
Priests and zealots in your realm whose faith fears the heavens will have their opinion of you changed by §R-25§! for §Y5§! years §Y(Heretic)§!

Watching the sky at night, you begin to notice movements that keep no pattern at all. Some stars appear and vanish at odd hours. Morrslieb waxes when every table says it should wane. Once, for the space of a breath, you could swear something vast passed between you and the stars. You must study this more...

The sky above your observatory is never still. Stars wink out and kindle again, Morrslieb swells and shrinks as it pleases, and in the shifting lights you see the shapes of plans within plans. The Architect of Fate is writing, and you have begun, very faintly, to read.
That star there vanishes whenever I look directly at it.

One morning your [GetFromRelation] [From.GetTitledFirstName] comes to see you, clutching a charm of [From.Religion.GetRandomGodName]. 'I am frightened for you,' [From.GetSheHe] says. 'They say you stay up in that tower until dawn, that you speak in riddles to people who are not there, and that you watched the Chaos moon all through Geheimnisnacht. That is how witches begin. Please, stop this before the hunters come.'
I am only admiring the beauty of the stars.
There are strange things out there and I need to see them!
What you heard are lies.

The studies you have conducted in your observatory have convinced you that there are many strange things beyond the known heavens. Yet there are few sources, and no one you dare share them with. Then a travelling bookseller mentions an old collector in Remas, one Gianetto Zucaro, who is said to own books the Celestial College would burn.
I will go and see him.
No, this frightens me. I should stop.
The Liber Caelestior

You arrive at the crumbling palazzo of the collector, old Gianetto Zucaro. After some persuasion he lets you in, and you speak late into the night among towers of mouldering books. He tells you of Necrodomo the Insane, who saw the coming of the Ruinous Powers in the stars and wrote it all down in the 'Liber Caelestior', the Celestine Book of Divination, before he clawed out his own eyes. Impressed by your sincerity, Zucaro offers to sell you a copy. He warns you, though, that the book has a way of finding the minds that read it too closely... and that its owners seldom keep it long.
Yes, I must have it!
No, thank you.

Working in your observatory, you are often disturbed by scratchings in the walls, uncannily large insects carrying away small pieces of your equipment, and hunched figures that watch you from the rooftops and are gone into the night before you can confront them. You struggle to keep your mind on the work.
I must focus!
It's no use, I should give this up.

The Liber Caelestior has proven a key to many locks. Necrodomo charted the stars as no one before him, and his tables fit the sky better than any you have owned. But between the tables are other pages: verses that rhyme only when read backwards, drawings of things with too many angles, and a prophecy of the End of All Things that you are beginning to believe. A level of understanding that might make one... mad.
I should leave it on the shelf for now.
I must delve deeper!

Great wisdom comes to those who study the world and learn from it. Your studies of the stars and the things beyond them have taken you down very strange paths, and your learning has grown beyond measure since that first night at the lens.
The stars are right!

You are finally certain, absolutely certain. There are things you understand now that lie beyond the ken of ordinary [Root.GetMenWomen]. The sky is a thin veil, and behind it the Realm of Chaos waits and watches and hungers. If they knew, oh, if they knew! But it is the task of scholars such as you to keep such things secret, lest the whole world go mad with the knowledge of how small it is.

You are finally certain. You have seen the threads of fate run across the heavens and knot together in the Realm of Chaos, and you have seen your own thread among them, bright and twisting. The Changer of Ways has shown you a sliver of His design. Others would go mad with it. You only smile.

You are finally certain. The Plan of the Old Ones is written in the stars, and so is the wound in it: the Rift at the poles, the green moon that came through it, the long night that waits at the end of the count. The Slann have known this for ten thousand years. Now you know it too, and you understand why they so seldom wake.

You are finally certain, and you wish you were not. The ancestors read the stars to count the seasons, but they never looked at the gaps between them. You have. Something waits out there that is older than the Ancestor Gods and hungrier than any grudge. Better it go into a sealed book than into the mouths of the young beards.
I shall be a devoted keeper of these secrets.
I will hide this and dedicate myself to other things.

Shortly after the death of your [GetFromRelation] [From.GetTitledFirstNameWithNick], strange news reaches you. [From.GetHerHisCap] library was broken into in the night, and the only thing taken was an old book bound in black leather, of Tilean make. Two servants who were in the library at the time were found dead. The witnesses refuse to describe the state of the bodies, and the priest who saw them has not spoken since.
Strange...
The Liber Caelestior

The 'Liber Caelestior' or Celestine Book of Divination, written by Necrodomo the Insane. Its star tables are the finest ever made, and between them lie prophecies of the End Times and truths that eat at the mind of whoever reads them.
The Liber Caelestior
This character owns a copy of the Liber Caelestior of Necrodomo the Insane.
This character has built an observatory and spends every clear night watching the Sun's road, the two moons and the stars.
This character has proven that the Known World turns about the Sun.
This character has looked into the strange lights between the stars, and keeps what they saw to themselves.
